prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 time-reversal-invariant topological insulator, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state

statement.case_for: I keep B030 as my preferred single-part prize after the full exchange, but I narrow the citation. The Kane-Mele papers introduced the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall effect, and Molenkamp's group observed edge transport in HgTe/CdTe wells that matched the prediction. That is a classic prediction-then-observation chain, and it has been confirmed by independent groups and materials for about fifteen years with a stable interpretation. Round 1 showed that the support is broad: Danielsson prefers it, and Eriksson, Mehlig, Lindroth and Olsson each say they would not oppose it or keep it as an alternative. The citation should name the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator in the form the three laureates established, and it should not claim the whole field of topological insulators. That wording leaves the 3D materials work to be recognised, or not, as a separate achievement.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, raised by Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Eriksson, is attribution. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp tested, and Hasan led the 3D observations. Any three names omit someone with a real claim. The 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions also gives the committee a second argument that topology has already been honoured. I accept that B021 has the cleaner theory-plus-experiment split and that its three supporters hold a firm first place. I weigh that against its youth and its unsettled mechanism, but I do not claim B030 is free of difficulty. Its credit problem is real and the citation can only disclose it, not remove it.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B021 first because its attribution is cleaner, and says B030 needs more than three names and must be argued as distinct from the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree that B021 attributes more cleanly, and I do not dispute that Bistritzer belongs with MacDonald. On the 2016 point, I think the committee can separate the two prizes. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz covered topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall state, which break time-reversal symmetry. B030 is a time-reversal-invariant phase classified by a Z2 index. Its first-principles prediction and observation are a separate achievement. On names, I would rather have a defined trio with an honest limit than force a four-name credit that the rule does not permit. I do not change my ordering because of cleanliness alone, since the mechanism of superconductivity in magic-angle graphene is still debated and the field is eight years old.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B021, keeps B030 as his first alternative, and still doubts that Mele is the right third name against Hasan.
responses.response: My view of Mele has not moved, and I want to say why. The Z2 invariant and the graphene quantum spin Hall proposal came from the two joint Kane-Mele papers. Taking Mele out for Hasan would split a single theoretical contribution in half, and the citation would then credit a prediction to one person and an observation of a different phenomenon, the 3D insulator, to another. Hasan's work is important, but it is a second step, and if the committee wants to honour it I think it should be argued as its own part. I accept that this leaves a visible omission. I note that Mehlig's own words keep B030 as a first alternative, so our difference is about ordering, not about the science.

responses.point: Kroll asks why I ranked B024 sixth, whether the reason is proximity to the 2005 and 2012 prizes or the narrow sense of discovery, and how lattice clocks differ from those prizes.
responses.response: Both reasons applied, and I put more weight on the second than I should have. Reading Kroll and Lindroth, I accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea from the comb or from single-ion control, so proximity to 2005 and 2012 is a weaker objection than I stated. My remaining hesitation is that the headline payoff, a redefinition of the second or a new-physics limit, has not yet arrived, and that Ludlow, Lemonde, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and RIKEN groups carry part of the 10^-18 milestone. Because the credit for Katori and Ye is the cleanest on the shortlist, I now list B024 as an alternative in place of the optical-lattice simulation ballot. I would not put it first this year, but I take the case seriously.

responses.point: Danielsson defends Mele as inseparable from Kane and argues that the 3D materials should be a distinct achievement and not a substitute for Mele.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of this argument and share it. We should say plainly in the discussion record that BHZ and Hasan are omitted and that the three-person rule forces this. Where I go slightly further is on the wording: the citation should say 'quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulator' and should not read as a prize for 3D topological materials. If a colleague still thinks the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a visible injustice, as Johansson does, I cannot answer that completely, but I think the proposal-and-first-observation chain is still the most defensible reading of who made the decisive contribution.

responses.point: Johansson would revisit B030 if colleagues could show that the BHZ role is adequately covered by the three-name credit.
responses.response: I cannot show that BHZ is fully covered, and I will not claim it is. What I can say is that BHZ predicted the effect in a specific material and that this prediction relied on the Kane-Mele framework, while Molenkamp's observation was the decisive experimental test. The three-name credit follows the originating prediction and the first observation of the effect. I also note that Johansson's own B006 faces a comparable boundary around Wineland-lineage and Monroe-type work, which he accepts and handles through citation wording. I think the same approach applies here, with the omission disclosed and the citation kept narrow.

responses.point: Olsson moved from two names to three on B021 and says she would not oppose B030 but sees the omission of Hasan or the BHZ authors as hard to defend.
responses.response: I appreciate that she would not oppose it. Her move to three names for B021 shows the same logic I apply to Mele: a joint paper should not be split to keep a prize small. Her point on Yuan Cao for B021 and mine on BHZ for B030 are of the same kind, and I think neither makes its candidate unawardable. The committee has to choose which omission it is more willing to record. I put the omission in B030 as one of the second step in the field and not of the original prediction.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and of Hasan for B030, since the three-person rule leaves them out and the citation can only disclose that.

Whether eight years is too early for B021 relative to fifteen years for B030. Three members hold B021 first and I cannot show their weight on maturity is wrong, only that I weigh the open mechanism and the parallel experimental groups more heavily.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize is close enough to B030 to count as an overlap despite the distinction by time-reversal symmetry.
I rely on my memory of priority chronology and not on verified sources, and I have no expertise in condensed matter beyond what I can judge from the shortlist evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle group) do not involve any credited name on the shortlist. As chair I have a stated preference for B030, and I have tried to summarise the other positions faithfully in the round-1 chair summary. My own field is experimental astroparticle physics, so I rely on colleagues for condensed-matter and quantum-optics judgments.
